newsitem.title: USA: Ill. road funding may be $2 bln short over 5 years.
newsitem.headline: Ill. road funding may be $2 bln short over 5 years.

text.p: Illinois' failure to reach an education financing accord last month could also lead to major road and mass transit repair problems in the next five years, state Transportation Secretary Kirk Brown said Tuesday.

After focusing on Gov. Jim Edgar's failed tax swap plan for education funding and property tax cuts, lawmakers had little left to consider raising the Illinois gasoline tax or vehicle licensing fees to provide more money for repairs, Brown said.

Without new revenue sources, Illinois will fall more than $2 billion short of funding needed to maintain the 17,000 miles of highways overseen by the Illinois Department of Transportation in the next five years, Brown said.
Mass transit funding will also see a 40 percent dropoff in the five year period, Brown added.

Illinois can maintain the debt service on the $1 billion of bonds issued for transportation projects over the last seven years, but cannot issue any more debt under the current financial climate, Brown said.

"No business is going to go out and borrow money while facing future declining revenues unless the borrowing can help you increase your revenue stream and it obviously doesn't do that for us," Brown said.
Illinois lawmakers approved a $1.05 billion construction budget for fiscal 1998, down from $1.2 billion in 1997 in the session concluded Saturday, Brown said.

Projected construction spending over the next five years is $4.8 billion -- about $2.2 billion less than needed to maintain roads and $3 billion less than necessary for restoring highway expansion plans, Brown said.
The transportation department stopped approving new road expansion plans two years ago when faced with funding troubles that will only increase under current spending limits, Brown said.

The state gasoline tax and vehicle licensing tax fund the department's capital expenditure programs. The department has not received an increase in the gasoline tax in eight years or in the vehicle licensing tax in 14 years, Brown said.

"All the suburban communities looking for solutions to congestion problems and urban areas looking for four-lane highways, it's just not possible," Brown said. "You can't start adding on to your system when you don't have enough money to maintain what you have."
Brown said he does not believe lawmakers will address transportation funding needs until they complete an education financing reform plan.
